source.title: Assessing Intelligence in Artificial Neural Networks
source.authors: Nicholas J. Schaub; Nathan A Hotaling

record.tranche_reason: Trains two LeNet architectures with partially and fully randomized MNIST labels and reports accuracy, but does not report training error against the randomized targets.
record.gate_note: The randomized-label experiments report accuracy without specifying whether it is measured on train or test data; the text says accuracy was measured on both data sets without randomized labels. The study does not report fit to the randomized targets. Mentioned Zhang et al. results are cited prior work and are not rows. Batch normalization and dropout results concern neural efficiency and accuracy, not the versions’ random-label claims.
record.test_reason: The study measures clean-label accuracy as MNIST training-label corruption increases, directly testing V4's degradation component. Section 4.3 explicitly identifies the large networks' 75% results as test accuracies, resolving part of the record's evaluation-set uncertainty. It does not report training accuracy against corrupted targets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately describes the authors' interpretation: high-aIQ networks resist memorization and overtraining, retaining substantial clean-label accuracy under 75% label corruption. Their broader conclusion promotes state-space efficiency and aIQ for selecting smaller networks. However, the reported clean-label accuracies do not directly demonstrate resistance to fitting randomized targets.
record.recipe_differences: Two MNIST LeNet architectures with batch normalization were trained at selected high-aIQ and highest-accuracy configurations; the paper does not reproduce the original random-label fitting measurement. Uses L2 weight regularization and SGD with Nesterov updates; random-label results used batch normalization.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with architecture and selected network: high-aIQ networks retain higher reported accuracy than largest networks at 25%-75% randomized labels; both perform poorly at 100%.
record.problems: Only two LeNet architectures on MNIST are studied. Randomized-label table does not identify whether reported accuracy is train or test, and accuracy is measured against unrandomized labels, so it cannot establish fitting of randomized targets. The random-label tables report no uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error against completely randomized targets, with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters. Chance clean-label accuracy alone cannot establish this.
Relative training time and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit to corrupted targets and the resulting joint claim of retaining signal while memorizing noise. Only five corruption levels are reported, so behavior between them is unmeasured.

Random-label fitting under weight decay, dropout, and augmentation, and generalization after removing explicit regularization. The dropout experiments retain L2 regularization and do not measure random-target fit.
Within-training ordering of real-pattern learning and noisy-label memorization.

missing.what: EMNIST accuracy after MNIST training at 0% versus 75% corruption: large LeNet-300-100, 76.21% versus 24.93%; small LeNet-300-100, 58.43% versus 55.46%; large LeNet-5, 90.56% versus 34.16%; small LeNet-5, 89.36% versus 74.67%. These extend the noise-degradation comparison to a separate evaluation dataset.

record.verdict_notes: The record's limits_scope verdict treats missing training-fit measurements as an adverse result; those measurements belong under untested. Section 3.3 says both clean train and test sets were evaluated. Table 3 lacks an explicit split caption, but Section 4.3 identifies the large-network 75% entries as test accuracies, and its zero-corruption small-network entries match Table 2's explicitly test-set results. Reading the full table as test accuracy is therefore well supported, though partly inferred. No random-label fitting failure can be inferred from chance accuracy against original labels.

versions.untested_parts: Whether training error on completely random labels reaches zero or near zero, whether test error is at chance, and whether this occurs without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time relative to true labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Whether training error remains perfect on the corrupted targets; the reported accuracy is on unrandomized labels, and the text does not specify train versus test for Table 3.
Whether regularization prevents fitting random labels or whether removing it harms true-label generalization.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

tranche.reason: The study tests degradation under randomized training labels using selected batch-normalized LeNet architectures and clean-label accuracy, without measuring interpolation of corrupted targets.

source_check.notes: Accuracy was evaluated against unrandomized labels, so these results do not establish fitting of corrupted training targets or resistance to such fitting. The corruption tests used three replicates per model, but Table 3 reports no uncertainty; uncertainty is reported for other experiments.
